account: A tech company that the authors do not name gave its AI Navi app free to about 500 taxi drivers, about 6% of drivers working for taxi firms in Yokohama, from 3 to 31 December 2019. The app suggested routes where demand was predicted to be high. Kyogo Kanazawa, Daiji Kawaguchi, Hitoshi Shigeoka and Yasutora Watanabe, economists at the University of Tokyo, compared each driver's cruising time with and without the app turned on, holding place and hour fixed. They report that the app shortened the search for customers by 5% on average and by 7% for low-skilled drivers, with a near-zero effect for high-skilled drivers. The 2022 working paper puts the narrowing of the productivity gap at 14%, and the version that Management Science published in February 2026 puts it at 13.4%. Drivers chose when to turn the app on, which the authors address with fixed effects and an instrument based on how unfamiliar the driver was with the area. More than half of the drivers offered the app never tried it. The study covers one city for one month. The company supplied the data, the authors report no financial support from it, and Japanese public research agencies funded the work.

ai_role.statement: The authors compare cruising time with and without the app on, within the same driver, place and hour, and use instruments for when drivers turn it on, which isolates the app's contribution under their assumptions.
